newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-LEGENDS STEAL SKI SPOTLIGHT.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-LEGENDS STEAL SKI SPOTLIGHT.

text.p: The Alpine world skiing championships finally experienced some of the excitement officials had been waiting for on Friday.
But the spark wasn't provided by Deborah Compagnoni or Alberto Tomba but by a skier who retired from competition almost a decade ago -- Sweden's Ingemar Stenmark.

What may have been the largest crowd to attend a race at these championships turned out in brilliant afternoon sunshine to watch the 'Legends of ski racing' test themselves against each other and Father Time.

While many on the start list did not really qualify for legendary status, there were enough of the sport's all-time greats, including Austrians Franz Klammer and Toni Sailer, to generate the enthusiasm the championships had been lacking.

Looking much the same as he did when he was dominating the World Cup circuit, despite having only skied five times this season, Stenmark crossed the finish line into the type of post-race media frenzy that is now generally reserved for Tomba or Luc Alphand.
Television camera teams fought for the best angles and reporters scuffled for quotes.
"There is such a big difference now with the skis," said Stenmark, who now lives in Monaco not far from Pernilla Wiberg. "It's impossible to compare the world championships now and when I raced."
Stenmark, who not surprisingly tips Wiberg to win the women's giant slalom, was unable to add a Legends' victory to a resume that includes a record 86 World Cup wins.
He settled for fifth behind Sailer, the oldest man in the competition at 61. The 1956 triple gold medallist took advantage of his time handicap to claim the biggest payday of his career -- a new car.
Switzerland's Vreni Schneider, just two seasons removed from the World Cup circuit, looked as if she could rejoin the Swiss women's team -- who have not won a world title since she left -- tomorrow.
She won the women's Legends' race and, unfortunately, only a new scooter.
